                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)

Transfer entropy (Schreiber, 2000) measures directed predictive coupling: how
much knowing the past of a source series $X$ reduces the uncertainty about the
future of a target series $Y$, over and above what the target's own past
already tells. With $Y_{t+\ell}$ the target $\ell$ steps ahead,
$Y_t^{(k)}$ the target's last $k$ values and $X_t$ the source's current
value,

$$T_{X \to Y} = H\big(Y_{t+\ell} \mid Y_t^{(k)}\big) -
  H\big(Y_{t+\ell} \mid Y_t^{(k)}, X_t\big),$$

measured in bits. It is zero when the source adds nothing to the target's own
history, and it is not symmetric: $T_{X \to Y}$ and $T_{Y \to X}$ are separate
quantities. Because it conditions on the target's past, a process with strong
momentum does not inflate it the way it inflates a plain lagged association.

Transfer entropy answers a different question from lag sequential analysis.
An adjusted residual says whether the transition $i \to j$ occurs more or less
often than base rates predict, and its sign says which. Transfer entropy says
how much information one series carries about the next step of another, and
it has no sign: a source that makes the target's next state less likely is as
informative as one that makes it more likely. The two are read together, as
this guide shows. `transfer_entropy()` is marked experimental in the package.

```{r package}
library(lagdynamics)
```

## Data

- **`engagement`**: weekly engagement states (`Active`, `Average`,
  `Disengaged`) of 138 students over 15 weeks, one row per student; two rows
  are entirely missing.
- **`group_regulation`**: coded regulation actions in 2,000 collaborative
  learning sessions, one row per session and one column per ordered time
  point (`T1` to `T26`), nine states.
- **`ai_long`**: a long log of 8,551 coded behaviours of an AI coding
  assistant in 428 "vibe-coding" sessions from 34 projects, in which a person
  builds software by instructing the assistant in natural language. Each row
  is one coded behaviour, ordered within its
  session by `order_in_session`. The column `code` holds one of eight
  behaviour codes (`Ask`, `Delegate`, `Execute`, `Explain`, `Investigate`,
  `Plan`, `Repair`, `Report`) and the column `cluster` the broader category
  the code belongs to (`Action`, `Communication`, `Repair`).

## The estimator

`transfer_entropy()` computes plug-in Shannon entropies from pooled
(target future, target history, source value) triples. Each sequence
contributes the triples that fit inside it, so the lag never crosses from one
sequence into the next, and triples with a missing value are dropped. The
returned table has one row per ordered pair with the columns:

- `te`: the transfer entropy in bits.
- `te_normalised`: `te` divided by the target's leftover uncertainty
  $H(Y_{t+\ell} \mid Y_t^{(k)})$, so it is the share of what the target's
  own past leaves unexplained that the source explains (0 to 1).
- `te_effective`: `te` minus the mean transfer entropy of the surrogates, a
  bias-corrected value (surrogate test only).
- `p`: the surrogate p-value (surrogate test only).
- `n`: the number of pooled triples.

Rows are ordered by decreasing `te`. The arguments `lag` ($\ell$, default 1)
and `history` ($k$, default 1) set the prediction horizon and the length of
the target's own past.

## A state network from one sequence dataset

Given one set of categorical sequences, `transfer_entropy()` returns a
directed network among the states. Each ordered pair of states $s \to r$ is
turned into two binary series: the source is "the unit is in $s$" and the
target is "the unit is in $r$". The transfer entropy of the pair is then the
information that being in $s$ now gives about being in $r$ next, beyond
whether the unit is in $r$ now. Self-pairs are not computed, so $K$ states
give $K(K-1)$ rows. The call below skips the significance test.

```{r engagement-te}
transfer_entropy(engagement, test = "none")
```

The largest flows end in `Disengaged`: knowing whether a student is `Active`
this week gives 0.036 bits about whether the student is `Disengaged` next
week, 6.0% of the uncertainty that the student's own disengagement status
leaves. Flows into `Average` and `Active` are five to eight times smaller
(0.007 and 0.005 bits). The rows come in identical pairs. This is a property
of the binary decomposition with three states: once the target's own
indicator says the student is not `Disengaged`, the student is either
`Active` or `Average`, so the two source indicators carry the same
information. The documentation of `transfer_entropy()` notes this
redundancy; with three states the network has three distinct values, one per
target, and a larger alphabet or the bivariate mode below is needed for
source-specific flows.

## Testing against surrogates

A plug-in estimate of transfer entropy is positive even when the source and
the target are unrelated, because sampling noise always produces some
apparent information. The surrogate test (`test = "surrogate"`, the default)
shuffles the source values across the pooled triples `R` times, which breaks
the coupling between source and target while keeping both marginal
distributions, and recomputes the transfer entropy each time. The p-value is
$(1 + \#\{T_\text{surrogate} \ge T_\text{observed}\}) / (R + 1)$, and the
effective transfer entropy subtracts the surrogate mean. `seed` makes the
shuffles reproducible.

```{r engagement-surrogate}
transfer_entropy(engagement, R = 199, seed = 2026)
```

The four flows into `Disengaged` and `Average` exceed all 199 surrogates
($p = 0.005$, the smallest attainable value), and the two flows into `Active`
exceed all but one ($p = 0.010$). The bias correction is small: the
effective transfer entropy of `Active -> Disengaged` is 0.0357 bits against
an estimate of 0.0365, because 1,734 triples leave little room for noise. The
directed flows are real, and the flow towards disengagement is the one of
practical size.

## Longer history and longer horizon

The `history` argument conditions on more of the target's own past.

```{r engagement-history}
transfer_entropy(engagement, history = 2, test = "none")
```

With two weeks of the target's own status known, the flows into `Active` and
`Average` shrink to between a quarter and an eighth of their size (from
0.0048 to 0.0013 bits into `Active`, from 0.0070 to 0.0009 into `Average`), while the flow into `Disengaged` barely moves
(0.0338 bits). Most of what the current state said about the next active or
average week was already contained in the student's own recent history; what
it says about the next disengaged week is not. The `lag` argument moves the
prediction horizon in the same way as in `lsa()`; `lag = 2` asks about the
state two weeks ahead.

## A larger alphabet

With nine states the binary channels are no longer redundant and each
ordered pair carries its own value. The call below lists the strongest flows
of the `group_regulation` network.

```{r regulation-te}
regulation_te <- transfer_entropy(group_regulation, test = "none")
head(regulation_te, 8)
```

The strongest flows run from `consensus` to `plan` (0.059 bits) and from
`emotion` to `cohesion` (0.058 bits). Among these eight flows,
`discuss -> synthesis` has the largest normalised value: it explains 23.5% of the leftover uncertainty about
whether the next action is a synthesis, against 7.5% for
`consensus -> plan`. The surrogate test is omitted here: its cost grows with
`R` times the number of ordered pairs, which is 72 for nine states.

The lag sequential analysis of the same data gives the signs.

```{r regulation-lsa}
transitions(lsa(group_regulation), significant = TRUE,
            sort = "strength") |> head(6)
```

`emotion -> cohesion` is a strong flow in both analyses and over-represented
($z = 58.2$): emotional expressions are followed by cohesion. `discuss -> plan`
is the third largest flow of information (0.046 bits) but the most avoided
transition of the table ($z = -36.9$, 46 observed against 962 expected): a
discussion predicts that the next action is *not* planning. Transfer entropy
ranks the two among the most informative relations of the network; only the
residual says that one is an attraction and the other an avoidance. Read
transfer entropy for the strength of directed dependence and the adjusted
residual for its direction.

## Two aligned series

When `y` is supplied, `transfer_entropy()` computes the full-alphabet transfer
entropy between two aligned series, in both directions. The two series must
have the same shape: the same number of sequences and the same length within
each. In `ai_long` every coded behaviour carries both its `code` and its
`cluster`, so the two columns are aligned by construction. The log is ordered
by session and by position within session, and the columns are passed as one
long series each.

```{r bivariate}
with(ai_long, transfer_entropy(code, cluster, R = 199, seed = 2026))
```

The coupling is one-directional. The code of the current behaviour carries
0.0715 bits about the cluster of the next one beyond what the current cluster
says ($p = 0.005$). The reverse flow is exactly 0: the cluster is a function of
the code, so the current cluster cannot tell anything about the next code that
the current code does not already tell. The negative effective value
($-0.0098$) is the bias correction applied to a true zero. Passed as one long
series, the 8,550 pairs include the 427 that join the last behaviour of one
session to the first of the next, about 5% of the total; a series per session
(one row per session, `NA`-padded) avoids them.

## Transfer entropy and lag sequential analysis

| | Lag sequential analysis | Transfer entropy |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Does $i \to j$ occur more or less than base rates predict? | How much does the source's present tell about the target's future beyond the target's own past? |
| Sign | Signed: over- or under-represented | Unsigned: attraction and avoidance both count |
| Conditioning | On the margins of the transition table | On the target's own history (`history`) |
| Unit | $z$, odds ratio, probability | Bits, or a share of leftover uncertainty |
| Test | Normal reference, bootstrap, permutation | Source-shuffling surrogates |
| Function | `lsa()`, `transitions()` | `transfer_entropy()` |

Use lag sequential analysis to name the transitions that occur more or less
than expected and to test them. Add transfer entropy when the question is
which states carry predictive information about others once each state's own
persistence is accounted for, and when a process has strong momentum, as the
`engagement` data do. Report transfer entropy with the surrogate p-value and
next to the signed residual, never on its own.

## References

Schreiber, T. (2000). Measuring information transfer. *Physical Review
Letters, 85*(2), 461-464.
